francis.title: The Wolf of Gubbio
francis.story: A wolf has been attacking livestock around Gubbio. The town is armed and terrified. Francis does not join the hunt. He walks out beyond the walls to meet the animal himself, calling it “Brother Wolf,” and asks it to make peace with the people who will then feed it.

challenge.prompt: What does this teaching story say Francis offered first?
options: Blessing the hunters from the walls so they could finish the job
Fasting until the wolf starved outside the town
Meeting the wolf in the open and speaking peace instead of force
Promising that God would strike the wolf if it returned
challenge.hint: Francis treats the wolf as a creature, not an enemy to erase.
challenge.explanation: The Gubbio story is a beloved teaching tradition, not a courtroom history. It shows Francis meeting fear with mercy that also protected the town — peace that asked something of both sides.

francis.funFact: Later tellings say the wolf lived among the people of Gubbio until it died of old age.

francis.title: Brother Sun, Sister Moon
francis.story: Near the end of his life Francis is almost blind, in pain, and staying in a hut near San Damiano. Instead of cursing the darkness, he composes the Canticle of the Creatures — praise of God through Brother Sun, Sister Moon, Brother Wind, and even Sister Death.

challenge.question: When did Francis compose the Canticle of the Creatures?
choices: On the day he first stripped off his father’s cloth in the square
While nearly blind and ill, late in his life
During the Fourth Lateran Council, as a hymn for bishops
As a battle song for the crusade he hoped to join
challenge.hint: The song comes from weakness, not from a triumph parade.
challenge.explanation: The Canticle is praise born in suffering. Francis thanks God through creation while he can barely see it — that is Franciscan joy, not a nature hobby.

francis.title: Rebuild My Church
francis.story: Praying before the crucifix at the ruined chapel of San Damiano, Francis hears the words, “Francis, go and rebuild my church, which is falling into ruin.” He does not draft a speech for Rome. He sells cloth, carries stones, and starts repairing the little chapel with his own hands.

challenge.prompt: What is the first thing Francis does with that call?
options: Rides to the pope to demand a reform council
Writes a rule for knights before touching a stone
Waits until a bishop puts the order in writing
Begins the dirty work of repairing a falling chapel
challenge.hint: He takes the words literally before he understands them fully.
challenge.explanation: Francis starts with the chapel in front of him. Only later does the Church read a deeper meaning: rebuild the Body of Christ through poverty, peace, and example. Holiness often begins with the next small repair.

francis.title: Franciscan Gifts
francis.story: Francis did not walk alone. Clare, Anthony, and Bonaventure each carried a different gift inside the same poor, joyful family. Matching them is a way of seeing how one call branches.

challenge.prompt: Match each Franciscan saint to the gift most tied to their memory.
challenge.hint: Think song, cloister, preaching, and teaching.
challenge.explanation: One founder, many gifts. Francis sang praise, Clare built a hidden life of poverty, Anthony preached, and Bonaventure gave the family a mind as well as a heart.

francis.funFact: The Franciscan family today includes hundreds of thousands of friars, sisters, and lay members across its branches.

carlo.title: The Exhibition That Traveled
carlo.story: As a teenager in Milan, Carlo spends hours building a website that gathers documented Eucharistic miracles from around the world. He wants classmates — and strangers on the far side of the planet — to know that the Host is not a symbol only.

challenge.question: What did Carlo catalog on the website he built?
choices: Rankings of Italy’s holiest parishes
Eucharistic miracles from many countries
Cheat codes for the video games he loved
His private diary of mystical visions
challenge.hint: The site was a classroom, not a fan page.
challenge.explanation: Carlo used ordinary web skills to teach an extraordinary claim: Christ is truly present in the Eucharist. The exhibition drawn from his research has been shown on every continent.

carlo.title: A Computer in the Kingdom
carlo.story: Carlo liked soccer, video games, and coding. He also went to daily Mass and stood up for classmates who were bullied. He did not treat the internet as a toy to hide, or as a pulpit for fame. He treated it as a tool that could carry truth farther than he could walk.

challenge.prompt: How did Carlo treat the internet?
options: As something holy people should never touch
As a stage for becoming a famous Catholic influencer
As a tool for friendship and teaching the faith
As a place to argue until the other person quit
challenge.hint: He neither fled technology nor worshipped it.
challenge.explanation: Carlo’s witness is not “computers are sacred.” It is that a teenager can use the same tools as everyone else — with charity, honesty, and a clear purpose.

carlo.title: A Short Life
carlo.story: In 2006 Carlo is diagnosed with leukemia. He offers his suffering for the pope and for the Church. He dies in Monza at fifteen. Years later the Church raises him to the altars — not because his life was long, but because it was faithful.

challenge.question: How old was Carlo when he died?
challenge.hint: He never finished high school.
challenge.explanation: Carlo died at fifteen in 2006. The Church honors the density of a life, not its length. His feast is kept on October 12.

carlo.title: A Lasting Legacy
carlo.story: Fifteen years can still hold a clear path. Put Carlo’s life in order and you see an ordinary boy whose love of the Eucharist kept widening.

challenge.prompt: Arrange these moments from Carlo’s life in chronological order.

events.text: Born in London to Italian parents
Receives First Holy Communion in Milan
Beatified by Pope Francis in Assisi

challenge.hint: Birth, Communion, website, death, then the Church’s recognition.
challenge.explanation: The dates are simple: 1991, 1998, 2002, 2006, 2020. What is not simple is a teenager who treated the Eucharist as the center of a short, bright life.

carlo.funFact: Carlo was canonized in 2025. His exhibition of Eucharistic miracles has been translated into dozens of languages.

joseph.title: The Just Man
joseph.story: Matthew says Joseph is a just man. When he learns Mary is with child, he does not expose her to public shame. He plans to divorce her quietly. Then an angel speaks in a dream: the child is from the Holy Spirit. Joseph wakes and takes Mary as his wife.

challenge.question: Before the angel spoke, what did Joseph plan to do?
choices: Bring her before the elders for judgment
Divorce Mary quietly, to spare her public shame
Leave Bethlehem that night without a word
Ask Herod to decide the matter
challenge.hint: Matthew calls him just — and his first instinct is mercy.
challenge.explanation: Joseph’s first move is protection, not reputation. Then he trusts the dream and stays. Justice in this story is not cold; it is careful love that refuses to harm.

joseph.title: Up in the Night
joseph.story: After the Magi leave, an angel warns Joseph in a dream: Herod wants the child dead. Joseph does not wait for morning meetings. He rises at night, takes the child and his mother, and goes to Egypt until it is safe to return.

challenge.question: Why does Joseph take Mary and the child to Egypt?
choices: Census rules requiring every carpenter to register in Alexandria
The Magi invite the family to travel east with them
The angel in a dream warns that Herod wants to kill the child
Mary asks to visit relatives along the Nile
challenge.hint: The Gospel of Matthew names a dream and a king’s violence.
challenge.explanation: Joseph’s courage is quiet and fast. He believes the warning and moves his family. Responsibility here looks like a night journey, not a speech.

joseph.title: The Silent Saint
joseph.story: The Gospels record no spoken sentence of Joseph. We see him decide, work, dream, and protect. His holiness is in what he does when no one is taking notes.

challenge.prompt: What does Joseph’s silence invite us to practice?
options: Never speaking about God at all
Waiting for a public platform before serving anyone
Leaving hard decisions to louder people
Faithfulness that shows up in work and protection, not speeches
challenge.hint: Silence here is not emptiness. It is action without applause.
challenge.explanation: Joseph’s virtue does not need a microphone. He stays, he works, he protects. A life can preach without a quotable line.

joseph.title: Two Feasts, One Man
joseph.story: The Church keeps Joseph twice: March 19 as husband and guardian of the Holy Family, and May 1 as St. Joseph the Worker. The same man is remembered for the home he guarded and the trade he practiced.

challenge.prompt: Match each feast or title to what the Church is honoring.

pairs.right: Husband and guardian of the Holy Family
Joseph the Worker, dignity of labor
The trade Matthew’s neighbors would have known

challenge.hint: One date is the household. One date is the workshop.
challenge.explanation: Joseph is not only a statue in a side chapel. The Church honors both his hidden family duty and the ordinary work that fed that family.

therese.title: The Little Way
therese.story: Thérèse enters Carmel at fifteen and dies at twenty-four. She never founds an order or crosses an ocean. She discovers that holiness is not a ladder of great deeds. It is doing the next small thing — a smile, a hidden chore, a patience — with great love.

challenge.prompt: What is the heart of Thérèse’s “little way”?
options: Only heroic public deeds count as real sanctity
Holiness grows through small acts done with great love
You must leave your family to be close to God
God’s love has to be earned by never failing
challenge.hint: She looked for the smallest stair, not the tallest monument.
challenge.explanation: Thérèse taught spiritual childhood: trust, hidden love, and ordinary faithfulness. The little way is demanding because it leaves no hour off the hook.

therese.title: Doctor at Twenty-Four
therese.story: Thérèse writes her story under obedience. After her death the pages travel farther than she ever did. In 1997 St. John Paul II names her a Doctor of the Church — one of the few women to hold that title, and the youngest.

challenge.question: Why was Thérèse named a Doctor of the Church?
choices: She governed a diocese from Lisieux
She wrote a complete systematic theology in Latin
Her teaching on ordinary love shaped the whole Church
She was the first woman to enter Carmel
challenge.hint: Doctor here means teacher of the Church, not a university chair.
challenge.explanation: A Doctor is named for enduring teaching, not for academic rank. Thérèse’s little way changed how millions imagine holiness — including missionaries she never met.

therese.title: Offering the Day
therese.story: In the convent Thérèse is often cold, tired, or misunderstood. She does not wait for a grand martyrdom. She offers the day’s pinpricks — a wet laundry, a sister’s noise, her own irritation — as small sacrifices of love.

challenge.prompt: How does Thérèse treat daily frustrations?
options: As proof that God has forgotten her
As reasons to withdraw from community
As tests she must hide so she looks holy
As small offerings that can be given in love
challenge.hint: She does not need a crisis to practice sacrifice.
challenge.explanation: The little way baptizes the ordinary. A hard hour can be given; it does not have to be dramatic to be real.

therese.title: Doctors of Love
therese.story: Four women Doctors of the Church — Thérèse, Teresa of Ávila, Catherine of Siena, and Hildegard — each taught the Church in a different key. Matching them is a way to hear the chord.

challenge.prompt: Match each woman Doctor to the teaching she is most known for.

pairs.right: The little way of spiritual childhood
The Dialogue and bold counsel to popes
Visions, music, and writings on creation

challenge.hint: Childhood, castle, dialogue, creation.
challenge.explanation: The Church does not have one woman’s voice. Thérèse’s hidden love sits beside Teresa’s map of prayer, Catherine’s public courage, and Hildegard’s wide seeing.

therese.funFact: Thérèse remains the youngest person ever named a Doctor of the Church.

kolbe.title: Two Crowns
kolbe.story: As a boy, Raymund Kolbe later said, he saw Mary offer him two crowns — one white for purity, one red for martyrdom. He said he would accept both. The rest of his life reads like a long yes to that answer.

challenge.question: What did young Kolbe say when offered the two crowns?
choices: He asked to choose only the white crown
He would accept both
He refused, saying he was too young
He asked to trade them for a soldier’s sword
challenge.hint: The story is not about picking the easier gift.
challenge.explanation: Whether one reads the vision as history or as a later spiritual memory, Kolbe’s life matched the answer: he lived consecrated, and he died in another man’s place.

kolbe.title: In Another Man’s Place
kolbe.story: In Auschwitz, after a prisoner escapes, the camp chooses men to die. One of them, Franciszek Gajowniczek, cries out for his wife and children. Kolbe steps forward and asks to take his place. He is locked in a starvation bunker with the others.

challenge.question: Why does Kolbe step forward in the camp?
choices: To become a block leader and soften the rules
To bargain for extra bread for his barracks
To die in the place of a stranger who has a family
To escape with the man who had already fled
challenge.hint: He does not save himself. He offers a substitution.
challenge.explanation: Kolbe’s last act is concrete: one man lives because another stood in his place. Teach this as sacrificial love. The camp’s cruelty does not need graphic detail.

kolbe.title: The City of the Immaculata
kolbe.story: Years before the war, Kolbe founds Niepokalanów in Poland — a “city” of friars with printing presses. They publish a daily paper and magazines that reach hundreds of thousands. He fights bad ideas with better ones, not with silence.

challenge.prompt: How did Kolbe use the press before the war?
options: To print only private prayers for the friars
To publish anonymous attacks on his enemies
To raise money for a political party he led
To spread Marian devotion and Catholic truth at huge scale
challenge.hint: Niepokalanów was famous for its newspapers, not its silence.
challenge.explanation: Kolbe believed media could form a culture. He used ink the way some use a pulpit: to put Mary, the Gospel, and courage in ordinary hands.

kolbe.title: From Vision to Gift
kolbe.story: Kolbe’s path runs from a boyhood offering, through a publishing city, to a bunker. The order of those years is part of the witness.

challenge.prompt: Place these events from Kolbe’s life in order.

events.text: As a boy he later recalls Mary offering two crowns
Founds the Militia Immaculatae in Rome
Volunteers to die in another prisoner’s place

challenge.hint: Crowns, militia, priesthood, the city, then the camp.
challenge.explanation: The dates climb toward 1941. What they show is a long preparation: a man who had already given himself away before the last hour asked for everything.

kolbe.funFact: Franciszek Gajowniczek survived the war and attended Kolbe’s canonization in 1982.

bernadette.title: The Lady at the Grotto
bernadette.story: In 1858 a poor, asthmatic girl named Bernadette sees a lady in the grotto at Massabielle. Local officials press her. Parish priests doubt her. She does not decorate the story. She repeats what she saw, even when she does not understand it.

challenge.prompt: When adults doubted Bernadette, what did she do?
options: Changed details until the mayor was satisfied
Kept telling the same simple account without adding drama
Refused to speak to anyone, including her parish priest
Claimed she had always known the lady’s name
challenge.hint: Her holiness here is honesty under pressure.
challenge.explanation: Bernadette’s first virtue at Lourdes is not eloquence. It is fidelity to what she was given, without improving it for an audience.

bernadette.title: A Name She Did Not Know
bernadette.story: Bernadette asks the lady her name. The answer is, “I am the Immaculate Conception.” Bernadette is not a theologian. She has to repeat the strange phrase carefully so she will not forget it. The title was defined by the Church only four years earlier.

challenge.question: Why is the lady’s name a problem for Bernadette?
choices: She had already published a book on the dogma
She thought the lady was asking to be baptized
She did not understand the title and had to memorize the words
She refused to say any name but her own
challenge.hint: The words were bigger than the girl’s schooling.
challenge.explanation: The scene matters because Bernadette is not performing theology. A poor child carries a title she cannot explain — which is one reason the parish took it seriously.

bernadette.title: Mud, Then Water
bernadette.story: The lady tells Bernadette to drink from the spring and wash. Bernadette scrapes the dry ground. At first there is only mud on her face, and the crowd laughs. Then water comes. Lourdes will become a place of pilgrimage and healing — but the first act looks foolish.

challenge.question: What happens when Bernadette obeys the command to drink?
choices: The river instantly splits the rock with no digging
She refuses, afraid of looking foolish
The mayor’s men dig the spring for her that night
She digs in dry ground, is mocked, and a spring appears
challenge.hint: Obedience looks embarrassing before it looks miraculous.
challenge.explanation: The spring is born in a moment of public awkwardness. Bernadette’s yes is not glamorous. That is often how God begins a mercy people can later touch.

bernadette.title: Leaving the Spotlight
bernadette.story: After the apparitions, Bernadette does not become a celebrity guide at the grotto. She enters the Sisters of Charity at Nevers, lives with illness, and asks to be forgotten. The shrine grows. The visionary hides.

challenge.prompt: What does Bernadette do after Lourdes becomes famous?
options: Stays at the grotto as the official interpreter of every miracle
Enters religious life and lives quietly, away from the crowds
Tours Europe giving paid lectures on the lady
Returns to the cave each year to demand new messages
challenge.hint: She did not build a platform on the apparitions.
challenge.explanation: Bernadette’s later life is the other half of the story: the girl who saw Mary chose hiddenness. Fame was never the point.

bernadette.funFact: Bernadette’s feast is April 16, the day of her death in 1879. Our Lady of Lourdes is kept on February 11.

padrepio.title: The Long Line
padrepio.story: At San Giovanni Rotondo, people wait hours — sometimes days — to confess to Padre Pio. He is known for being blunt, for seeing through excuses, and for staying in the confessional long after a reasonable man would have stood up.

challenge.question: What was Padre Pio most famous for in his daily ministry?
choices: Writing a newspaper that attacked his critics
Spending long hours hearing confessions
Refusing to see anyone who was not a priest
Traveling the world as a concert preacher
challenge.hint: The line outside the box is the clue.
challenge.explanation: Whatever else is told about Padre Pio, the ordinary miracle of his life is mercy spoken one soul at a time. Confession was the work, not a side chapel.

padrepio.title: The Best Weapon
padrepio.story: Padre Pio said, “Prayer is the best weapon we have; it is the key to God’s heart.” He did not mean a last resort when every other plan failed. He meant the first move when anxiety, work, or pain arrived.

challenge.question: What did Padre Pio call prayer?
choices: Duty reserved only for people who cannot work
Something that replaces going to confession
The best weapon we have, and the key to God’s heart
Something useful only after you have tried everything else
challenge.hint: He used the language of a key and a weapon — not a hobby.
challenge.explanation: For Padre Pio, prayer is how a person enters the fight and how a person rests. Worry is not solved by more worry; it is carried to God.

padrepio.title: A Hidden Sharing
padrepio.story: In 1918, while praying, Padre Pio received the stigmata — wounds like Christ’s — which he bore for fifty years. He did not advertise them. Church authorities investigated him, restricted him, then later cleared him. He asked people to look at Jesus, not at him.

challenge.prompt: How did Padre Pio want people to treat the stigmata?
options: As proof that they should never go to a doctor
As a stage trick to grow his following
As a reason to skip Mass if they had seen him once
As a hidden sharing in Christ’s suffering, not a spectacle
challenge.hint: He pointed away from himself.
challenge.explanation: The Church does not require anyone to be fascinated by the stigmata. Padre Pio’s own counsel is safer: pray, confess, endure, and look at Christ.

padrepio.title: A Capuchin’s Tools
padrepio.story: Rosary, confessional, Mass, obedience — these were the tools of Padre Pio’s day. Matching them keeps the legend attached to the work.

challenge.prompt: Match each part of Padre Pio’s life to what it meant.

pairs.right: Hours of mercy, one person at a time
The prayer he called a weapon
The town where he lived and served

challenge.hint: Place, habit, prayer, and the box.
challenge.explanation: Padre Pio’s story is not a catalog of marvels. It is a Franciscan priest who stayed put, prayed, and heard the truth people were afraid to say.

johnpaulii.title: The Prison Visit
johnpaulii.story: On 13 May 1981, Mehmet Ali Ağca shoots John Paul II in St. Peter’s Square. The pope nearly dies. In 1983 he goes to Rebibbia prison, sits with his attacker, and speaks with him privately. He later says he has forgiven him.

challenge.question: What does John Paul II do after surviving the attack?
choices: Refuses ever to speak Ağca’s name again
Visits his attacker in prison and offers forgiveness
Asks the court to add years to the sentence as a lesson
Leaves Rome permanently for safety in Poland
challenge.hint: Mercy here has an address: a prison cell.
challenge.explanation: Forgiveness did not erase justice — Ağca remained in prison. It did refuse the last word to hatred. That is the Gospel John Paul II had been preaching made visible.

johnpaulii.title: Be Not Afraid
johnpaulii.story: At his inauguration in 1978, the new pope looks out over the square and says, “Be not afraid. Open wide the doors to Christ.” It becomes the sentence of his pontificate — spoken to a century that had many reasons to be afraid.

challenge.prompt: What did John Paul II ask the Church to do with its fear?
options: Never feel afraid, because fear is always a sin
Leave public life so the Church would be safer
Open the doors to Christ instead of closing them in fear
Trust only in political power to protect the faith
challenge.hint: The famous line is paired with opening doors, not with denial.
challenge.explanation: “Be not afraid” is not a scolding. It is an invitation: let Christ in, then walk into the century with hope. Courage, for him, is a form of trust.

johnpaulii.title: The Young Church
johnpaulii.story: John Paul II invents World Youth Day and spends himself on young people — not as a mascot, but as a pastor who believed they could carry a demanding faith. He told them they were not an accident of the times.

challenge.prompt: What was new about John Paul II’s care for the young?
options: He lowered every teaching so it would be easier to like
He asked the young to wait until middle age to live the Gospel
He replaced parishes with stadium events and nothing else
He created World Youth Day and preached a demanding hope to them
challenge.hint: He gathered them — and he did not shrink the faith to keep them.
challenge.explanation: World Youth Day is a gathering, not a gimmick. John Paul II trusted young people with the whole Gospel: mercy, purity, courage, and mission.

johnpaulii.title: A Long Pilgrimage
johnpaulii.story: Karol Wojtyła’s life runs from occupied Poland to the chair of Peter to a funeral the world watched. The years themselves preach.

challenge.prompt: Arrange these events from John Paul II’s life in order.

events.text: Elected pope and takes the name John Paul II
Dies in the Vatican after a long public illness

challenge.hint: Birth, election, the attack, death, then the altar.
challenge.explanation: 1920, 1978, 1981, 2005, 2014. A boy from Wadowice became a pilgrim pope whose last lesson was how to suffer in public without losing hope.

johnpaulii.funFact: John Paul II was the first non-Italian pope in 455 years and one of the most traveled popes in history.
